title: JSON Safeguards + Tool Routing Playbook — Demo with Asterion Labs
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood JSON mode, schema guardrails, tool/function calling for drug-interaction and internal KB routing. Discussed PHI constraints, on-prem options, and runtime fallbacks. Agreed next steps: share pilot checklist, security doc, and sample repo + schedule a benchmark run in 2 weeks.
topics: Tool/function calling patterns (internal drug-checker, KB search)
Runtime routing and fallbacks (hosted vs private)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel, Liam Chen (Redwood); Dr. Elena Ruiz, Samir Kapoor, Anya Petrov (Asterion Labs)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
Redwood did demo showing json-mode and how to force typed responses and call internal tools. Customer asked about PHI and private deployment, and about what happens when model returns invalid JSON. Showed fallback to safe text output and model variant routing. Next steps were sharing security pack and scheduling pilot benchmarks.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. I'm Maya from Redwood. we have Liam with me who'll run through the deep part. quick round?
[00:12] Dr. Elena Ruiz: thanks, Elena here, head of ML at Asterion. we're building a clinical decision support UI, so structured outputs are important — and obviously PHI concerns.
[00:20] Samir Kapoor: Samir, platform, i'll be owning infra integration.
[00:24] Anya Petrov: Anya, product, focused on success criteria and UI contracts.
[00:28] Liam Chen: great, quick agenda: show JSON mode live, schema guardrails, tool calling for our drug-interaction checker and KB lookup, then runtime fallback patterns and Optimize tips.
[00:40] Dr. Elena Ruiz: sounds good. one quick thing — we need enforcement: if response doesn't match schema, it must not reach the UI.
[00:48] Liam Chen: totally, we'll demo how the runtime validates and can reroute to a safe summarizer or a stricter model, plus a hard reject path.
[00:56] Speaker 1: (mumbling) also interested in latency impact when we add validation.
[01:02] Liam Chen: good q, we'll show both p95 and p50 tradeoffs in the console later.
[01:10] Maya Patel: okay i'll share my screen, starting with the API playground.
[01:25] Liam Chen: here we are — invoking the Redwood API in JSON mode. prompt has a schema: patient_id string, findings array of objects, each object fields: code, severity (enum), suggested_actions array of typed actions. you see we attach an enforcement level: warn | strict | strict_reject.
[01:48] Anya Petrov: can you show a real example with our drug-check tool?
[01:52] Liam Chen: yes — watch: model responds, then runtime runs a tool call: internal_service.drug_interaction_check({patient_med_list}) — if tool returns high_risk it annotates suggested_actions with urgent_referral and inserts a trace id.
[02:12] Dr. Elena Ruiz: what's the trust boundary? does the model get PHI? we can't send raw patient identifiers to hosted models.
[02:20] Liam Chen: good catch — two options: private deployment where data never leaves your VPC, or tokenization where we hash identifiers before contacting hosted models. Also we have a policy to keep tool calls inside your network if you wire up the private tool connector.
[02:38] Samir Kapoor: what's the latency on tool-calls? our local drug-check is sub-ms but calling model then tool seems to add round trips.
[02:46] Liam Chen: runtime supports sync and async tool patterns. for latency-sensitive flows we recommend local tool-first routing: check drugs first in platform, then only call model for synthesis. for when model calls tool, we can parallelize calls and prefetch — Optimize will recommend batching windows for that pattern.
[03:08] Maya Patel: i want to demo a failure scenario — model returns invalid JSON (this happens).
[03:14] Liam Chen: executing now. request -> model returned malformed JSON: missing closing bracket, key spelled sevrity. runtime validation flagged it. with enforcement=strict_reject we return a structured error and call fallback_summarizer to provide a plain text summary to UI.
[03:35] Anya Petrov: so UI can render error state and also show fallback summary?
[03:40] Liam Chen: yes. we attach a reason code and confidence score. UI can choose to surface or hide details.
[03:48] Dr. Elena Ruiz: whats the risk if fallback is plain text? product wants deterministic fields for downstream logic.
[03:54] Liam Chen: for that workflow we suggest keeping strict_reject for downstream processing, and have a parallel compensating workflow: send the same input to a smaller, deterministic model (we call it a scaffolding model) or run a rules-based extractor on the fallback text. Redwood Optimize can suggest which model family to use based on your token length and SLOs.
[04:18] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) how does the KV cache interact with schema enforcement?
[04:23] Liam Chen: K V cache — yeah sometimes transcribed as Kay V — basically cache prefixes and tool call results can be cached. schema enforcement runs on the assembled output all together. if a cached prefix would cause invalid shape, the runtime can skip cache for that request.
[04:40] Samir Kapoor: we're also trying to keep costs bounded. what levers do we have?
[04:45] Maya Patel: batching, quantization, model routing by cost tier. Optimize will run experiments on your pilot traffic and recommend batch sizes and a quantization profile (8-bit vs 4-bit) that preserve quality on your prompts.
[05:03] Liam Chen: example — for high-throughput background jobs we route to quantized variants; for fast UI responses use GPU-backed full-precision with small batch windows. we have automatic fallback: if dedicated capacity is saturated, requests route to a cheaper hosted variant or to a blocking path depending on policy.
[05:27] Anya Petrov: show me the Console view for these rules.
[05:30] Liam Chen: switching — Console -> Model Routes -> Policy editor. here you can define route by tag: latency_sensitive, PHI_protected. you can attach constraints: region, capacity tier, and model_variant. here's a canary rollout example where 10% goes to new-schema-model and 90% stays on stable.
[05:54] Dr. Elena Ruiz: can we see audit logs for tool-calls? legal wants end-to-end traceability.
[05:59] Liam Chen: yes — per-request trace id, token-level cost breakdown, tool-call timestamps and responses (redacted if needed). you can configure retention and integrate with your SIEM.
[06:16] Speaker 1: question about SSO and RBAC for console access.
[06:20] Maya Patel: we support SAML/SSO and granular RBAC. for private deployments you can sync with your IdP and lock down console. KMS integrations and HSM are available for key management.
[06:31] Samir Kapoor: any SOC2 evidence we can get?
[06:34] Maya Patel: yes — we'll share our security pack. also if needed there is an option for a compliance review and a private package with enhanced auditability.
[06:45] Dr. Elena Ruiz: curious about model debugging, how to reproduce a bad JSON output?
[06:50] Liam Chen: we have a prompt replay and eval harness. Console allows you to pin a prompt set, run batch replays, and see token-level logits in the debug play. you can also run counterfactuals with different temperature/seeds.
[07:05] Anya Petrov: show the tool calling schema — what happens if tool is down?
[07:10] Liam Chen: circuit breakers — runtime supports retries, fail-open, fail-closed. policy can specify fallback to a static rule-based response or to call an alternate tool endpoint. in demo, I flip the tool to down and the runtime reroutes to a cached last-known-good result.
[07:30] Speaker 2: (inaudible) what about data residency?
[07:33] Maya Patel: we can pin region and also do private deployment for on-prem. for EU-only workflows we advise private or dedicated with region locking.
[07:44] Dr. Elena Ruiz: who's the recommended start for pilot? cost, timeline, evaluation metrics?
[07:50] Liam Chen: pilot typically 4–6 weeks: week 0 onboarding and security sign-off, week 1–2 run small traffic tests and schema tuning, week 3 run full benchmark and Optimize experiments, week 4 review. success metrics: schema validity rate > 99.5%, p95 latency < 400ms for UI flows, cost/unit targets you define.
[08:14] Samir Kapoor: can we run a benchmark with our drug-check integrated?
[08:18] Maya Patel: yes, we'll need a sandbox connector from your side and an creds exchange for private tool calls or we can proxy via your VPC connector.
[08:28] Anya Petrov: what about fallback transparency for clinicians — we can't surface too many internal errors.
[08:33] Liam Chen: you can choose to surface only high-level states. we emit structured reasons but UI can map them to friendly messages. also we support a gray-box mode where clinicians get the fallback but it's tagged as 'auto-generated recommendation — verify'.
[08:48] Dr. Elena Ruiz: ok can you recap security posture for PHI?
[08:52] Maya Patel: options: 1) Private deployment (data never leaves VPC), 2) Tokenization + ephemeral IDs before calling hosted models, 3) Bring-your-own-key with KMS/HSM, 4) Retention controls and audit logs. we'll include a checklist.
[09:11] Liam Chen: demo continues — show a complex structured output with nested actions and function calls: model outputs an action list that triggers two tools in sequence: first disambiguate medication (kb.resolveMedication), then drug_interaction_check. all calls are logged and attached to the response.
[09:34] Speaker 1: are these tool calls synchronous in trace?
[09:37] Liam Chen: yes we surface them in the trace and you can view them in the Console timeline.
[09:42] Samir Kapoor: how hard to integrate with our existing service mesh?
[09:47] Maya Patel: we've seen teams use VPC peering, proxy connectors, or an on-prem agent. we have docs and a sample helm chart.
[09:55] Anya Petrov: any gotchas for schema evolution? our product will change fields over time.
[10:00] Liam Chen: Console supports schema versioning and runtime will coerce older responses or reject based on enforcement policy. you can run staged rollouts and automated tests against older clients.
[10:12] Dr. Elena Ruiz: ok, pricing — how do we estimate cost?
[10:16] Maya Patel: pricing for hosted is per token + per-tool-call unit; Dedicated is reserved monthly capacity. for pilot we'll provide a sample model for cost-estimate with your expected throughput. Optimize also estimates token counts post-batching.
[10:30] Speaker 2: (soft) competitor question — has anyone looked at ModelHub or CloudAI for same features?
[10:35] Maya Patel: yes — some customers evaluate other managed endpoints; our differentiation is production-grade guardrails, unified runtime across hosted/private, and the Optimize toolkit that recommends batch/quant settings tied to quality metrics.
[10:47] Anya Petrov: can you share a sample repo or workshop?
[10:50] Liam Chen: we'll share a demo repo that includes schema examples, tool connector stubs, and a small eval harness.
[10:58] Maya Patel: quick recap and next steps — we'll share security pack, pilot checklist, demo repo, and propose a date for the benchmark run.
[11:07] Dr. Elena Ruiz: sounds good. any blockers on our side? Samir: i'll need a network diagram and a credential checklist.
[11:15] Samir Kapoor: yes, and an approximate cost projection before exec review.
[11:20] Maya Patel: we'll include cost projection and sample benchmark results.
[11:25] Anya Petrov: can you include suggested UI error states for schema failures?
[11:28] Liam Chen: yes, sample mapping included in the repo.
[11:33] Speaker 1: thanks everyone.
[11:36] Maya Patel: thanks all, we'll follow up by Friday with artifacts.
[11:40] Meeting end.

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hearings (K V cache vs KV, some names slightly off), timestamps approximate.
